client-concentration-guide.html.text:
Client Concentration Risk Analyzer · guide

How much revenue from one client is too much, and what to do about it

Short answer: once one client is a quarter of your revenue, losing them hurts; once it is two-fifths, losing them can end the business. Those are rules of thumb, not law, but they are the levels at which lenders, buyers and insurers tend to start asking.

What to measure

  • Top-client share: the largest client's revenue divided by total revenue over the last 12 months.
  • Top-three share: the same for your three largest clients together.
  • Effective number of clients: one divided by the sum of squared shares. It tells you how many equal clients your book behaves like.
  • Trend: is the top client's share higher in the newer half of the year than the older half? Rising dependence is worse than a high but falling number.
  • Survivability: average monthly revenue without the top client against your monthly costs.

Why the answer is a range, not a verdict

A client that has paid on time for six years under a multi-year contract is not the same risk as one that arrived last quarter, and an invoice export cannot tell them apart. The analyzer reports shares and arithmetic, flags the levels people commonly use, and leaves the judgement about contract length and replaceability to you.

Reducing it without firing your best client

  1. Run the analyzer on the last 12 months, or node cli.mjs analyze invoices.csv --costs 24000.
  2. Add your monthly costs and read the "without the top client" line first.
  3. Grow the rest: raise rates on new work and productise a repeatable offer for a second segment.
  4. Ask the big client for a longer commitment or a retainer in exchange for the volume.
  5. Re-run monthly; a cron job with --fail-on warn tells you the month a client crosses your line.

Questions

How much revenue from one client is too much?

There is no fixed line. Lenders and acquirers commonly start asking about a client above 25% of revenue and often discount a business for one above 40%. What matters more is whether you could cover your costs without that client, which the tool tests if you give it your monthly costs.

Is a long contract enough to make concentration safe?

It helps, but it does not remove the risk: contracts end, get renegotiated, or are terminated for convenience. Treat a long contract as time to diversify, not as a reason not to.

What is the fastest way to reduce dependence on one client?

Grow everything else rather than shrinking the big client: raise your rate on new work, productise a repeatable offer for a second segment, and ask the big client for a longer commitment or a retainer in exchange for the volume.

No warranty. This guide is provided free and as-is, without warranty of any kind. It is not financial, legal or business advice, and lenders, buyers and insurers use their own criteria. Product names are trademarks of their owners and are used only to describe where numbers come from.

Best-effort hosting, no SLA. These tools are free, experimental, and may be slow, broken, moved, or taken offline without notice. Do not use this as a system of record.

Free and open source (MIT). Support is optional and never changes what the tool does.

CLIENT CONCENTRATION RISK ANALYZER · RUNS IN YOUR BROWSER

How much of your revenue could walk out the door with one client?

Paste your invoices — client, date, amount — and see every client's share of revenue, whether you are getting more or less dependent, and whether you would cover your costs without your biggest client. The same numbers a lender, buyer or insurer will look at.

Nothing is uploaded and no accounting tool is contacted. The text box is analysed in this browser and never leaves your device. The warning levels are common rules of thumb, not a standard, and you can change them.

1. Paste your invoices

2. What it found

Clients by share of revenue

ClientRevenueShare

Findings

RuleLevelDetail

Prefer a CLI, or want a monthly check?

Same logic, zero dependencies, one command — reads a file or stdin:

node cli.mjs analyze invoices.csv
cat invoices.csv | node cli.mjs analyze -
node cli.mjs analyze invoices.csv --costs 24000 --months 12
node cli.mjs analyze invoices.csv --warn-top1 20 --json --fail-on warn

Get cli.mjs and engine.mjs — Node 18+, nothing to install, no network call. Exit code 1 on a finding, so a cron job or CI step can tell you the month a client crosses the line. More: How much revenue from one client is too much, and what to do about it.

What's recognised

InputHandling

Warning levels are rules of thumb (25% / 40% for one client, 60% / 80% for the top three); invoice date, not payment date, is used; contract length, churn risk and how easily a client could be replaced are not modelled.

Common questions

Does this connect to my accounting software?

No. It reads the invoice rows you paste and never contacts QuickBooks, Xero, FreshBooks, Stripe or any bank. Every figure is arithmetic on the rows you gave it, so nothing here leaves your device.

How do I get the numbers?

Export an invoice or sales-by-customer report from your accounting tool and keep three columns: customer, invoice date and amount. A header row is read by name, so most exports paste as they are. Date is optional; with dates the last 12 months are used.

What counts as too concentrated?

There is no legal line. Lenders, acquirers and insurers each pick their own, and 25% of revenue from one client is a common level at which they start asking questions, 40% a level at which they often price the risk in. The tool uses 25/40 for one client and 60/80 for the top three as defaults you can change.

What is the effective number of clients?

One divided by the sum of each client's squared share. Ten clients of equal size give 10; one client at 70% and nine small ones give about 1.9. It says how many equal clients your revenue behaves like, which is a better guide than a raw count.

Is my data uploaded anywhere?

No. The browser page runs on the text in your own browser and never sends it anywhere. The CLI reads a local file or stdin and makes no network call.

No warranty. This tool is provided free and as-is, without warranty of any kind, express or implied. It is not financial, tax, legal or business advice. It does arithmetic on invoice rows you paste; it is not a credit assessment, a valuation or a forecast of whether any client will stay. Lenders, buyers and insurers use their own criteria. QuickBooks, Xero, FreshBooks and other product names are trademarks of their owners, used only to describe where numbers come from.

Best-effort hosting, no SLA. These tools are free, experimental, and may be slow, broken, moved, or taken offline without notice. We do not promise uptime, backups of anything you type, or that a URL will keep working. Do not use this as a system of record. If a tool needs to survive, get cli.mjs and run it yourself.

Everything runs in your browser. The text you paste is never uploaded; there are no accounts, cookies, or analytics vendors. Anonymous feature events (analyze_run, example_loaded) are counted only in local storage and can be deleted with the button below. Do Not Track and Global Privacy Control are honoured.

Related tools on the same repo: the Invoice Aging & Late Payer Analyzer, the Cash Runway Planner, the Client Profitability Time Analyzer and the Freelance Rate Increase Calculator.

Free and open source. If this saved you some guesswork, the code is under an MIT licence — support is entirely optional and never changes what the tool does.
